summary: TLS 1.3 fixes known weaknesses of TLS 1.2 and its use is growing. This document says that no further changes will be approved for TLS 1.2, except urgent security fixes, new TLS exporter labels, and new ALPN protocol IDs.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC limits future changes to TLS 1.2. It allows urgent security fixes and new entries in two named registries, but says post-quantum work will target TLS 1.3 or later.

questions: what is the tls 1.2 feature freeze
what changes are allowed for tls 1.2
subtitle: TLS 1.2 changes are limited, with exceptions for urgent fixes and two registries.

tldr.problem: TLS 1.3 fixes most known deficiencies of TLS 1.2, but both versions have extension points for new features.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC limits approved TLS 1.2 changes to urgent security fixes, new TLS Exporter Labels and new ALPN Protocol IDs.
tldr.outcome: The TLS Working Group will not specify post-quantum cryptography for TLS 1.2. This rule does not apply to DTLS.

facts.label: TLS 1.2 exceptions
facts.value: Urgent security fixes, Exporter Labels, ALPN Protocol IDs

today: RFC 9851 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2026. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The TLS 1.2 Feature Freeze
sections.content:
The RFC says TLS 1.3 fixes most known deficiencies in TLS 1.2. Examples include encrypting more traffic and removing most cryptographic primitives considered weak. It also says TLS 1.3 has robust security proofs.

Because both versions have extension points, new algorithms and supported groups could otherwise be added without defining a new protocol. This RFC says no TLS 1.2 changes will be approved except urgent security fixes determined by TLS Working Group consensus and the registry exceptions described below. The rule applies to TLS, not any version of DTLS.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC limits new changes to TLS 1.2, the Transport Layer Security protocol version. It does not set this limit for Datagram TLS.

sections.title: Post-Quantum Cryptography
sections.content:
The RFC says a cryptographically relevant quantum computer, if available, is likely to make RSA, finite-field Diffie-Hellman and elliptic curve cryptography much easier to break. It describes NIST's multi-year effort to standardize algorithms intended to be safe when such computers are feasible, and notes standards released by NIST in 2024.

The TLS Working Group's post-quantum work is focused exclusively on TLS 1.3 or later. The RFC states that post-quantum cryptography will not be specified for TLS 1.2.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC expects post-quantum cryptography work to target TLS 1.3 or later. It says the TLS Working Group will not define it for TLS 1.2.

sections.title: Changes to TLS Registries
sections.content:
The RFC does not close TLS registries. It changes the instructions to IANA and TLS Designated Experts about which entries may be added. New TLS Exporter Labels and ALPN Protocol IDs are not limited by this document.

Other TLS registries receive a note that entries added after IESG approval of RFC 9851 are intended for TLS 1.3 or later, with no similar requirement for DTLS. Entries should carry an informal indication saying For TLS 1.3 or later.
sections.plainLanguage: Most TLS registries now identify new entries as intended for TLS 1.3 or later. The Exporter Labels and ALPN Protocol ID registries are exceptions.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC describes itself as a security document and gives post-quantum security concerns as an additional reason to upgrade to TLS 1.3. It provides no separate security mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: The document's security reason is to move new cryptographic work to TLS 1.3 or later.
